pages.title: Meridian Commerce Platform
pages.summary: The big picture: the Meridian Commerce Platform shown as a single box, surrounded by the people who use it and the external systems it relies on.

sections.title: Overview
sections.body: Meridian is a direct-to-consumer commerce platform serving the EU market. It is owned and operated by the Platform Engineering group; identity, payments and email delivery are delegated to managed SaaS providers.
Click the **Meridian Commerce Platform** box to zoom into the container view, or any surrounding element to jump to its description below.

items.label: Security
items.note: Card data never touches our systems

items.label: Scalability
items.note: Horizontal pod autoscaling on all services

items.label: Observability
items.note: Traces, metrics and logs to Grafana stack

items.label: Privacy
items.note: Data residency in the EU; 30-day erasure SLA

pages.title: Meridian Fulfilment Platform
pages.summary: Everything that happens after payment: warehouse operations, carrier bookings and parcel tracking, shown as a single box with the people and systems around it.

sections.title: Overview
sections.body: The Fulfilment Platform runs the Malta distribution centre. It receives paid orders from the **Commerce Platform** as events, so the two systems can be released and scaled independently. Carrier integrations and financial postings are its only synchronous external dependencies.
**Customer** and **Email Delivery** also appear here; they are described on the [Commerce Platform context page](#/ctx-meridian).

pages.title: Commerce Core
pages.summary: The customer journey from browsing to payment: web front-ends, the gateway, the core domain services and their data stores.

sections.title: Overview
sections.body: The platform follows a service-per-bounded-context style. All synchronous traffic enters through the **API Gateway**; cross-service side effects are propagated asynchronously over Kafka. Each service owns its database — no shared schemas.

items: Two web front-ends, one gateway, three domain services and one worker.
Runtime: Kubernetes (EKS 1.31) with Istio mTLS between pods.
Search and reporting live in a separate container view: **Search & Insights**.

pages.title: Search & Insights
pages.summary: How customers find products and how operators see what is happening: the search stack and the reporting pipeline, both fed by domain events.

sections.title: Overview
sections.body: Search and reporting are **read models**: neither owns business data. Both are rebuilt from Kafka events, so a full re-index or reload is always possible without touching the core services.

pages.title: Warehouse Operations
pages.summary: From paid order to packed parcel: order intake, wave planning, picking and stock control inside the distribution centre.

sections.title: Overview
sections.body: Orders arrive from the Commerce Platform on Kafka and are turned into fulfilment orders. Inside the platform, services talk over **RabbitMQ**; stock movements are posted to the ERP asynchronously so a slow ERP never blocks the warehouse floor.

pages.title: Shipping & Tracking
pages.summary: From packed parcel to doorstep: carrier selection, labels and collections, and keeping customers up to date.

sections.title: Overview
sections.body: Every carrier sits behind the **Carrier Gateway**, so adding a carrier means adding one adapter. Tracking events flow back through the same gateway and are pushed to customers by email and the public tracking page.

pages.title: Order Service
pages.summary: Order Service owns the checkout use case and the lifecycle of an order from PLACED to FULFILLED.

sections.title: Overview
items: Hexagonal layout: controllers and adapters at the edges, domain logic in the centre.
**Checkout Service** is the single orchestrator; it holds no state between requests.
Events are written to an outbox table in the same transaction as the order.

pages.title: Payment Service
pages.summary: Payment Service wraps Stripe behind an internal contract, adding idempotency, risk scoring and soft-decline retries.

sections.title: Overview
items: Every authorisation is keyed by an idempotency key supplied by the caller.
Fraud scoring runs before any external call — high-risk payments never reach Stripe.
Stripe types never leak past the adapter (anti-corruption layer).

pages.title: Catalog Service
pages.summary: Catalog Service owns products, price books and the customer-facing view of stock.

sections.title: Overview
items: Writes go through **Product Manager**, which versions every change.
Available stock is a projection of inventory events — the catalogue never calls the warehouse.
Changes are published through an outbox, like Order Service.

pages.title: Search API
pages.summary: Search API answers product queries in under 100 ms at p95, applying merchandising rules on the way.

sections.title: Overview
items: Stateless; scales horizontally behind the gateway.
Ranking rules are data, edited by merchandisers in the Admin Console.
The index client fails fast and falls back to cached top results.

pages.title: Warehouse Service
pages.summary: Warehouse Service turns fulfilment orders into waves and pick tasks, and confirms dispatch.

sections.title: Overview
items: Waves are planned per carrier cut-off.
Pick paths are optimised per wave, not per order.
Packing confirmation is the trigger for shipping.

pages.title: Inventory Service
pages.summary: Inventory Service keeps an auditable stock ledger and handles reservations with expiry.

sections.title: Overview
items: Every change is a ledger entry; current stock is derived.
Reservations expire automatically if an order is cancelled.
Adjustments require a reason code for the audit trail.

pages.title: Shipping Service
pages.summary: Shipping Service chooses a carrier for each parcel, buys the label and books the collection.

sections.title: Overview
items: Rate shopping balances price against the delivery promise.
Labels are stored for 7 years for customs and disputes.
Carrier calls go through the gateway — no carrier SDKs here.

pages.title: Checkout & Place Order
pages.summary: A signed-in customer submits their cart. The order is priced, payment is authorised synchronously and an order.placed event is published.

items.label: Pre-conditions
items.value: Customer is authenticated; cart is non-empty

items.label: Post-conditions
items.value: Order persisted as PLACED; event published

steps.info: See the Payment Authorisation sequence for the internals.

pages.title: Payment Authorisation
pages.summary: Inside Payment Service: the request is de-duplicated, risk-scored and, if acceptable, authorised with Stripe via a PaymentIntent.

items.label: Post-conditions
items.value: PaymentIntent in requires_capture, or a local decline

steps.note: Declined locally — Stripe is never called

pages.title: Order to Dispatch
pages.summary: A paid order crosses from the Commerce Platform to the Fulfilment Platform, stock is reserved and the parcel is packed — or the order is back-ordered.

items.label: Pre-conditions
items.value: Payment authorised; SKUs exist in the warehouse

steps.note: Order joins the next wave before carrier cut-off

pages.title: Customer Sign-in
pages.summary: OIDC Authorization Code flow with PKCE, followed by the first authenticated API call that loads the account page.

items.label: Pre-conditions
items.value: Customer has an account with the IdP

pages.title: Order Confirmation Email
pages.summary: An order.placed event is consumed by the Notification Worker, rendered and delivered through SendGrid with bounded retries.

items.label: Pre-conditions
items.value: Customer has a verified email address

items.label: Post-conditions
items.value: Email accepted by SendGrid; offset committed

steps.note: After 3 failures the record goes to notifications.DLQ

pages.title: Decisions, Risks and Unknowns
pages.summary: What the diagrams do not show: the decisions behind the architecture, what could go wrong, and what is not known yet.

items.title: Kafka as the domain event backbone
items.body: Decouples notifications, analytics and fulfilment from the checkout path.

items.title: Kong as the single API gateway
items.body: Centralises JWT validation, rate limiting and request logging at the edge.

items.title: Database per service
items.body: Services own their schema; integration only via APIs and events.

items.title: Transactional outbox for events
items.body: Guarantees at-least-once publication without distributed transactions.

items.title: gRPC between Order and Payment
items.body: Strongly-typed contract with deadlines on the hot path.

items.title: OpenSearch for product search
items.body: Managed service, good facet performance, no licence lock-in.

items.title: ClickHouse for operational reporting
items.body: Column store keeps dashboard queries under a second at current volumes.

items.title: RabbitMQ inside the fulfilment platform
items.body: Work-queue semantics and per-message acknowledgement suit warehouse tasks better than a log.

items.title: Event-sourced stock ledger
items.body: Every movement is auditable; snapshots keep reads fast.

items.title: Offline mode for the scanner app
items.body: Associates keep working through Wi-Fi drops; tasks sync when back online.

sections.title: Risks
rows: **Order Service and Payment Service share one Kafka topic for retries.**
A poison message blocks both retry paths until it is skipped by hand.
**Catalogue cache has no expiry on price changes.**
Customers can see a stale price for up to an hour after a change.
**The notifier retries SendGrid without a back-off.**
A SendGrid outage turns into a burst of retries when it recovers.

sections.title: Unknowns
items: Who owns the Fulfilment platform's on-call rota is not documented.
The expected peak order rate behind the checkout SLA is not stated.

sections.title: Terms
rows: Architecture Decision Record: one decision, its context and its consequences.
Service Level Agreement: the availability or latency the business commits to.
Warehouse Management System: the fulfilment platform's stock and picking service.
